newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan markets come alive as dollar soars vs yen.
newsitem.headline: Japan markets come alive as dollar soars vs yen.

text.p: The dollar powered to a 42-month high against the yen in Tokyo trade on Monday, while Japanese government bonds scaled new heights and stocks broke a five-session losing streak.
The dollar strode over the psychologically important 113.60 yen hurdle to reach its highest level since April 1993, bolstered by aggressive sales of yen against major currencies.
"Since the dollar rose above 113.60 yen, there is no sign that the momentum will be halted," said Noriyuki Takano, assistant director of foreign exchange sales at Barclays Bank Plc in Tokyo.
The dollar, which ended at around 113.40 yen in New York on Friday, was trading as high as 113.96 yen in late afternoon.
The Tokyo stock market also rose, although dealers said the dollar's strength was only a minor factor.

The Tokyo stock market's key Nikkei average gained 145.44 points or 0.70 percent, but analysts were quick to play down talk of a rebound in the market -- which fell every day last week on post-election uncertainty -- as turnover was light.
"Trade was extremely dull today and the benchmark Nikkei's rise was feeble and not really strong enough to be considered a rebound," a broker at a second-tier brokerage said.
Brokers said investors were sidelined because of the unclear domestic political situation.

Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto's Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) is looking for partners for a coalition government, and analysts say failure to create a coalition would leave Hashimoto no option but to lead a minority government which could be weak and short-lived.
Shares in export-related firms showed muted reaction to the dollar's surge against the yen, as the market had mostly factored in the merits of a stronger dollar against the yen.
"The rise is too sudden," a strategist at Okasan Securities said. "A strong dollar is good for exporters, but prices of materials used to produce things can become costly and the merit is offset."

Domestic and overseas operators both dumped the yen on Monday. The view that Japanese monetary authorities will be forced to keep the official discount rate at a record low of 0.5 percent to strengthen Japan's economic recovery has made the yen an unattractive currency.
Factors such as these have accelerated sales of yen in favour of high-yielding currencies such as the Australian dollar and sterling, dealers said.

"Fundamentally, the crosses are leading the market, where the yen is definitely no good right now. There's some talk that European funds may be selling yen and Japanese stocks to switch to well-performing European currencies and stocks," said a U.S. bank dealer in Tokyo.

The dollar slumped to a post-war global low of 79.75 yen in April 1995 but has gradually regained ground against the Japanese currency, helped by rounds of central bank intervention and steps to encourage Japanse capital to flow into dollar-based instruments, as well as low interest rates.
Meanwhile, Japanese government bonds continued to rise into uncharted territory, with the December contract setting a new record high of 124.96 before easing back to close at 124.74.

The market has been rising recently because of a tight supply and demand balance, helped by speculation that funds arising from the wind-up of failed housing loan firms will eventually flow into the bond market.
